project.topic: What if 8.3 billion people on Earth sneezed at the same time?
project.title: What if 8.3 billion people on Earth sneezed at the same time?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If every person on Earth sneezed in the same second, what would actually happen in that blind moment?
project.viewer_takeaway: A synchronized sneeze shuts almost every human eye at once, but only for about a blink: traffic rolls a few metres and carries on, the sound arrives nearest first and fades, and a normal day probably holds about as many sneezes, just spread out.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Most healthy people sneeze a few times a day or less; sneezes are reflexes that usually close the eyes briefly and spray droplets a metre or two.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: At one instant every person on Earth sneezes once. Nothing else changes. The film follows one city crosswalk, the planet, and the city as heard from above.
assumptions: Eyes close for about 0.3 s during the sneeze (a fraction of a second; not precisely measured).
Traffic in the city moves at 50 km/h.
Animals do not sneeze on cue.
People, the dog and the crosswalk are illustrative.
causal_chain: Everyone sneezes in the same second.
Almost everyone’s eyes close reflexively, including drivers.
Moving cars cover a few metres with no human looking; animals, like the dog, still watch.
People sneeze while driving every day, so nothing systematic happens.
Sound from the sneezes arrives nearest first; farther ones are fainter and soon lost under traffic.
Up to ~330 trillion droplets fly out at once.
A normal day probably holds a similar number of sneezes, spread out.
In that second the only bystanders not sneezing are animals.
uncertainties: How long eyes stay shut during a sneeze varies and is not well measured.
How many vehicles are moving at any moment is an estimate (tens of millions of ~1.5 billion).
Distant sneezes are probably inaudible over traffic and through walls; only the nearest would be heard clearly.
Average sneezes per person per day are uncertain (most people sneeze fewer than four times a day).

claims.statement: The scenario has all 8.3 billion people sneeze in the same second.
Most people close their eyes reflexively when they sneeze, for a fraction of a second.
claims.reasoning: Physicians describe eye closure as part of the sneeze reflex; it is common but not universal.

claims.statement: With about 1.5 billion vehicles in the world, millions are moving at any moment; at 50 km/h a car covers about 4 m in 0.3 s.
claims.reasoning: Fleet size from Hedges & Company; 13.9 m/s x 0.3 s = 4.2 m.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Millions" and "a few meters", not a precise count.

claims.statement: Drivers routinely sneeze at the wheel; a sub-second eye closure is comparable to a long blink, so a synchronized sneeze would mostly pass without incident.
claims.reasoning: Everyday experience; a few metres of straight travel.

claims.statement: Sound travels about 343 m/s, so the sound of a sneeze 1 km away arrives about 3 s after nearby ones; a loud sneeze is about 90 dB up close, so only nearby sneezes would stand out over traffic.
claims.reasoning: Speed of sound in air at 20 C; loudness estimate from Bottom Line Inc; spreading loss of about 6 dB per doubling of distance.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narration says only nearest first, then fading; the HUD shows how far the sound has travelled, not what is audible.

claims.statement: A single sneeze can generate as many as 40,000 droplets, so 8.3 billion sneezes could release up to about 330 trillion.
claims.reasoning: BioNumbers entry citing Cole & Cook (1998); 8.3e9 x 4e4 = 3.3e14.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Up to" and "could top 300 trillion"; the HUD says UP TO.

claims.statement: More than 95% of healthy people sneeze fewer than four times a day, so a normal day worldwide probably holds on the order of 8 billion sneezes.
claims.reasoning: Hansen & Mygind (2002) diary study; an average near one sneeze per person per day is an assumption.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Probably a normal day"; the HUD shows an approximate count.

claims.statement: Animals are not part of the premise, so a dog would keep its eyes open and be the only bystander not sneezing at that instant.
claims.reasoning: Premise covers people only; comic illustration.
claims.presentation_guardrail: A joke about that one second.

creative_direction.logline: The countdown hits zero and everyone on Earth sneezes: for one blink only a dog watches the road, the sound arrives street by street, and the only one left to say bless you is the dog.
creative_direction.visual_identity: A sunny crosswalk at eye level with an elegant boxless countdown in the top-left, a POV blink to black, a glowing blind stretch on the road, sound rings over the city, slow-motion droplets in profile, and a twinkling planet.
creative_direction.lighting: Morning sun over the far side of the road.
creative_direction.camera_language: Handheld eye-level POV with a blink to black; curb-level replay and a dog-height close-up; a high aerial for sound; slow motion in profile; a push in on the dog.
creative_direction.motion_language: Comic timing from a countdown: a collective wind-up, one snap, recovery; real-speed traffic and sound; 12x slow motion for the spray.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metre scale on the street; true 343 m/s rings over a 2.3 km city; Earth radius 1 for the globe; droplets enlarged.
creative_direction.opening_hook: Every driver passing you sneezes the instant you do.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: Millions of drivers go blind for a blink while only a dog watches; nothing happens, the sound arrives street by street, and up to 300 trillion droplets fly at once.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: For once there is nobody left to say bless you, except the dog.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The film ends at the same crosswalk where the countdown began.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the street, humanoids, globe, lit puffs and sky rig; add a reusable dog-v1 and an editorial HUD style in overlay-labels-v1.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original light score: ticking tension under the countdown, a held breath, a big comic sneeze chorus, a bright groove for the city, a twinkling celesta for the day, and a one-bark button.
audio.sfx_direction: 0.3 s silence before the sneeze chorus; car pass-by; a rolling rumble of distant sneezes; slowed sneeze and mist hiss; a single bark.
